newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong's immigration chief row mars transition.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's immigration chief row mars transition.

text.p: A growing scandal over Hong Kong's former immigration chief has marred transition to Chinese rule and could spark a confidence crisis in the territory's bureaucracy, analysts said on Thursday.

The Hong Kong government admitted on Wednesday that Laurence Leung quit as Immigration Director after a graft probe uncovered misconduct, but has denied that his departure had anything to do with a breach of security.
Still, analysts said the scandal could trigger an exodus of officials who fear the quality of government would plummet after Beijing takes over on July 1.
"Some senior bureaucrats may decide to opt out," political analyst Sunny Lo of Hong Kong University said.

"Our surveys show more and more Hong Kong people are concerned about corruption, particularly in the Civil Service. The case of Laurence Leung proves such public concern is genuine. There is real, genuine anxiety," he said.
"This is something we could do without at this time of the transition," pro-democracy legislator Emily Lau told Reuters. "Hong Kong can't afford it."
"The last thing we want is this to sidetrack us from the details of the transition, the transfer of power," she said.
Many of Hong Kong's 6.3 million people fear Beijing could impose repressive rule or that China-style corruption could infect the territory.
Leung suddenly announced his early retirement in July for "personal reasons" but the government on Wednesday conceded he was pushed to leave because of doubts about his integrity.

Secretary for the Civil Service Lam Woon-kwong told the territory's Legislative Council that Leung had undisclosed shareholdings, a business liaison with a legislator, and an investment in a mainland China enterprise, and had violated rules on repayment of a government housing loan.
He had also failed an integrity test by the police. Leung was not charged with a criminal offence but was deemed unsuitable to continue in his highly sensitive position.
Political analyst Lo said even if post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa, who takes over on July 1, asks incumbent mandarins to remain in their posts, they might now not want to stay.
He said the case also heightened anxiety about whether Tung would play down corruption cases after the flag change.
"This is a very interesting incident and will definitely affect the Civil Service, particularly the disciplinary forces such as the Immmigration Department," analyst Lo said.
Legislator Emily Lau said the public was alarmed by the government's handling of the case and by its "China connection".

"The public perception is that there's something wrong with Leung, but they also disapprove of the way the government has handled it, and feel there's more that the government is not revealing," she said.
But if the inquiry shifted into the realm of security, the governmment would probably invoke its right to silence, she said.

Lau said given the approaching handover, Leung's China links were alarming. "The people he's doing business with are people with powerful connections in China -- this is politically a very highly charged subject."

China's reaction so far has been cautious and restrained. "We don't want to see things that are not beneficial to the smooth transition of the Civil Service," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang said in Beijing on Wednesday.
Anxiety permeated the editorials of major Hong Kong papers.
"Far from easing the disquiet raised by the removal of Laurence Leung from his post six months ago, yesterday's Legco hearing left the mystery intact in some major respects...
"We are faced with the spectacle of a government undermining its own credibility," the South China Morning Post said.

Pro-China politician Lau Siu-kai said Lam's reputation had also been tarnished by the way he had changed the government's story at the inquiry. "As a senior official his trustworthiness to the public is no doubt in question," Lau told reporters.
"Judging from the mauling Mr Lam took from legislators yesterday, suspicion of a political cover-up in the episode remains strong," said political commentator Chris Yeung.
